What are the definitions of the permitted values for Participation Status (RLA)?

Broadly, four patterns of test administration are allowed under the statute and regulations: 1) English language proficiency assessments; 2) locally selected, nationally recognized high school tests allowed under 34 CFR § 200.3; 3) schools participating in Innovative Assessment Demonstration Authority (IADA) pilot tests authorized in 34 CFR §§ 200.104-109, and 4) states that administer multiple end-of-course tests to fulfill ESEA high school testing requirements. The Participation Status permitted values allowed align with these types of test administration.
The types, with the exception of English language proficiency and Medical exemption, are explained in the Definitions section.
English language proficiency assessment – May be taken by English learner students who have been in the U.S. less than 12 months in lieu of the reading/language arts assessment.
For Medical exemption, see guidance below.
Who is considered to have a significant medical emergency?

Each state determines what constitutes a significant medical emergency. On March 29, 2004, the Department announced a policy that students who are unable to participate in the state assessment during the testing and make-up windows because of a significant medical emergency will not count against the school’s participation rate. A May 19, 2004, “Dear Colleague” letter provided additional guidance acknowledging that there may be circumstances beyond an LEA’s control when a student cannot be assessed at any time during the testing window due to a significant medical emergency (e.g., a student is hospitalized due to an accident). In these cases, the school or LEA should not be penalized for that student’s absence due to the documented significant medical emergency. Therefore, when determining the percentage of students taking an assessment, states do not have to include a student with a significant medical emergency in the participation rate calculation. States desiring to use this flexibility are responsible for determining what constitutes a significant medical emergency. This guidance is posted on the Department’s website at: ESEA Policy Letters to Stateshttps://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.ed.gov%2Flaws-and-policy%2Flaws-preschool-grade-12-education%2Fpreschool-grade-12-policy-documents%2Fesea-policy-letters-to-states&data=05%7C02%7Ckara.osmonson%40aemcorp.com%7Ce388a4238f474afc613408de10db031d%7C7a41925ef6974f7cbec30470887ac752%7C0%7C0%7C638966730035412045%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=ivhUc%2F%2FDtgRakoYzBL%2BCGazOoNzph0bAqSrWL0dy5MA%3D&reserved=0.
What if my state does not have a policy for exempting students due to significant medical emergency?
If the state does not have such a policy, do not report any students as having a significant medical emergency. Report all students as either participating or not participating.
Should the significant medical emergency reported in this file align with states’ responses to the Assessment Metadata Survey?

Yes. If a state has a policy for exempting students due to significant medical emergencies, the state should report this information in the survey and report the count of students who were exempt due to significant medical emergencies in this file. For example, if a state indicates they have a policy related to significant medical emergency in the survey, the state must report counts for significant medical emergencies in FS188.
How do I report assessment data for recently-arrived English learners?

If permitted by your state’s policy, recently-arrived English learnersRecently-arrived English learners are English learners who have been in the U.S. for less than 12 months. can take the English language proficiency assessment (ELP) in lieu of the reading/language arts assessment. If English learners take this assessment, they are reported in FS188 under the PARTELP value in Participation Status (RLA).

However, the performance of these students is included in FS050, not FS178. Therefore, the number of students reported as participants in FS188 will be higher than the number of students reported with results in FS178 by exactly the number of English learners who have been in the U.S. less than 12 month and who took the ELP in lieu of the reading/language arts assessment.
What grade levels should be reported?

LEA and school records should include all required grade levels that are present in the LEA or school. Reading/language arts assessments are required in grades 3 through 8 and once in high school. For example, a K-6 school should submit grades 3 through 6, but not 7, 8, and high school. See 34 CFR 200.2(a)(b)(1)(i).
State records must include assessment participation data for all required grades: 3 through 8 and once in high school.
Why do the permitted values include grades 9 through 12 as well as a value for “High School?”

The permitted values are provided so SEAs have more flexibility. For high school grades, assessment participation can be reported by specific grade levels or by using the permitted value for high school (HS). Data reported by specific grade levels (i.e., 9, 10, 11, and 12) or high school (HS) will be used for reporting participation in statewide assessments in high school. Do not report data using both specific grade level and the permitted value for high school (HS) for a specific assessment type. See 34 CFR 200.2(a)(b)(1)(i).
Please see question below about how to align grade levels reporting with the Assessment Metadata Survey.
How are assessments of students in grade 9 reported?

ESEA, as amended, requires states to administer assessments in reading/language arts in each of the grades 3 through 8 and at least once in grades 9 through 12. Students who took a reading/language arts assessment in grade 9 should be reported either as grade 9 or as high school. See 34 CFR 200.2(a)(b)(1)(i).
How should the grade levels reported in this file align with states’ responses to the Assessment Metadata Survey?

A state should report the same grade levels in FS188 that they report in the survey. For example, if a state indicates in the survey that it will report their regular assessments using the ‘HS’ permitted value, the state must also report using the ‘HS’ permitted value for that assessment type in FS188. The EDFacts Data Warehouse is unable to interpret data it receives unless it is an exact match to the corresponding metadata. See 34 CFR 200.2(a)(b)(1)(i).
How should the grade levels reported in this file align with grade levels reported in FS178?

A state should report the same grade levels in FS188 that they report in FS178. For example, if a state reported their regular assessment using the ‘HS’ permitted value in FS178, the state must also report using the ‘HS’ permitted value for that assessment type in FS188. See 34 CFR 200.2(a)(b)(1)(i).

States should use whichever permitted values best align with the major racial and ethnic subgroups used in the State’s accountability system as outlined in their Consolidated State Plan.

What if my state has a major racial and ethnic group that is not listed above?
SEAs should inform ED through PSC if the list above does not include all the major racial and ethnic groups used by the state.

What if some students are not assigned to a major racial and ethnic group? SEAs are required to report academic achievement data by the major racial and ethnic groups, as defined by the State. Some students in the State may not be included in a major racial and ethnic group. This file specification is used to report the number of all students who were enrolled during the state assessment testing window, by whether the students participated or did not participate in the state assessment in science.
For what assessments are data reported?

Report participation counts for the science assessment your State administers to meet the requirements of Section 1111(b)(2) of the ESEA. Section 1111(b)(2) of the ESEA requires States to administer statewide assessment to all students in science once in each of the following grade spans: grades 3 through 5, grades 6 through 9, and grades 10 through 12. These are the assessments the State must submit for ED’s peer review process for State assessment systems. If applicable, the State should report assessment data for those grades that the State uses in its Federal accountability system under ESEA Title I (section 1111(c)(4)(B)(i)((I).

If a State administers multiple science assessments in any of the grade spans for which it is required to administer a science assessment, the State should submit participation counts for ALL of the assessments it administers to meet the requirements of Section 1111(b)(2) and submits for ED’s peer review process for State assessment systems and ONLY the assessments it administers for this purpose. See also 34 CFR 200.2(a)(b)(1)(i).
Additionally, the assessment types reported in FS189 should be consistent with a state’s Assessment Metadata survey.
What students should be reported in this file?
Include all students enrolled during the testing window. This means include:

If a student was reported as taking an assessment in FS179, the student is also reported in FS189. This includes students who participated in any of the assessments listed in the Participation Statuses tables for Grade 3-9 and High School in Section 2.4.

Are students who were not enrolled for the full academic year reported?

Yes. Include both students who were enrolled for the full academic year and those who were not enrolled for the full academic year in this file. These data are used by a variety of sources, many of which do not differentiate on full year academic status. Please note that you are no longer required to disaggregate assessment data by “full academic year” and “non-full academic year” status. However, there is still an expectation that the assessment data will include students who were represented in both of these groups. See 34 CFR 200.2(a)(b)(1)(i).
Are all students reported in all category sets?

No. All students should be reported in category sets B (by sex (membership)) and in subtotal 1. For category set A (by major racial and ethnic groups), see question “what if some students are not assigned to a major racial and ethnic group” in section 2.5.3. For the other category sets, only include the students that meet the definition of the category being collected. For example, category set C collects information on children with disabilities (IDEA) by major racial and ethnic groups. Do not include students who do not meet the definition of children with disabilities (IDEA) in category set C. Please see section 2.5.5 of this document for additional information about reporting children with disabilities (IDEA) in this file. See 34 CFR 200.2(a)(b)(1)(i).

In the case where a student’s race/ethnicity or sex is unknown and/or cannot be reported using available permitted values, leave these students out of the relevant category set (either Cat Set A-Major Racial and Ethnic Groups) or Cat Set B-Sex (Membership)), but include them in the Subtotal.
Do any other file specifications collect related data?

If a student takes multiple assessments for a single grade or takes the same assessment multiple times, can all of those results be included in this file?

No. A student should be included only once for each subject area in each grade. For the purposes of reporting to EDFacts, a state should only report on the assessment system approved through the Department’s peer review process used to meet federal requirements for assessments and accountability, and should only report one score for that assessment. See 34 CFR 200.2(a)(b)(1)(i). For a student who takes the same assessment multiple times, the State should report the highest score.
How would “accommodations” be defined for the purposes of reporting?

Accommodations generally refer to adjustments to an assessment that provide better access for a particular test taker to demonstrate their true aptitude or achievement level and do not alter the assessed construct. These are applied to the presentation, response, setting, and/or timing/scheduling of an assessment for particular test takers. They may be embedded within an assessment or applied after the assessment is designed. Accommodations are provided in accordance with (for children with disabilities) the child’s IEP or 504 plan; and for some ELs, the appropriate EL team.
What are the definitions of the permitted values for Participation Status (MS)?
The types, with the exception of Medical exemption, are explained in the Definitions section. For Medical exemption, see guidance below.
Who is considered to have a significant medical emergency?

Each state determines what constitutes a significant medical emergency. On March 29, 2004, the Department announced a policy that students who are unable to participate in the state assessment during the testing and make-up windows because of a significant medical emergency will not count against the school’s participation rate. A May 19, 2004, “Dear Colleague” letter provided additional guidance acknowledging that there may be circumstances beyond an LEA's control when a student cannot be assessed at any time during the testing window due to a significant medical emergency (e.g., a student is hospitalized due to an accident). In these cases, the school or LEA should not be penalized for that student's absence due to the documented significant medical emergency. Therefore, when determining the percentage of students taking an assessment, states do not have to include a student with a significant medical emergency in the participation rate calculation. States desiring to use this flexibility are responsible for determining what constitutes a significant medical emergency. This guidance is posted on the Department’s ESEA Policy Letters to Stateshttps://www.ed.gov/laws-and-policy/laws-preschool-grade-12-education/preschool-grade-12-policy-documents/esea-policy-letters-to-states.
What if my state does not have a policy for exempting students due to significant medical emergency?
If the state does not have such a policy, do not report any students as having a significant medical emergency. Report all students as either participating or not participating.
Should the significant medical emergency reported in this file align with states’ responses to the Assessment Metadata Survey?

Yes. if a state has a policy for exempting students due to significant medical emergencies, the state should report this information in the survey and report the counts of students who were exempt due to significant medical emergencies in this file. For example, if a state indicates they have a policy related to significant medical emergency in the survey, the state must report counts for significant medical emergency in FS189.

LEA and school records should include all required grade levels that are present in the LEA or school. Science assessments are required for one grade in each of the following grade spans:

For example, a K-6 school would report one grade in the grade span 3 through 5. The school would include grade 6 science only if that grade is designated as a reporting grade level for the 6 through 9 science grade span.
State records must include assessment participation data for one grade in each of the three grade spans defined above. See 34 CFR 200.2(a)(b)(1)(i).
Why do the permitted values include grades 10 through 12 as well as a value for “High School?”

The permitted values are provided so SEAs have more flexibility. For high school grades, assessment participation can be reported by specific grade levels or by using the permitted value for high school (HS). Data reported by specific grade levels (10, 11, and 12) or high school (HS) will be used for reporting participation in statewide assessments in high school. Do not report data using both specific grade levels and the permitted value for high school (HS) for a specific assessment type. See 34 CFR 200.2(a)(b)(1)(i).

How are assessments of students in grade 9 reported?
For science assessments, ESEA groups grade 9 with grades 6 through 9. Science assessments taken in grade 9 should not be reported under the value for High School.

A state should report the same grade levels in FS189 that they report in EDPass. For example, if a state indicates in the survey that it will report their regular assessments using the ‘HS’ permitted value, the state must also report using the ‘HS’ permitted value for that assessment type in FS189. A state should report the same grade levels in FS189 that they report in FS179. States should use whichever permitted values best align with the major racial and ethnic subgroups used in the State’s accountability system as outlined in their Consolidated State Plan.

Do any other file specifications collect related data?

The purpose in collecting the identifier is to easily link charter schools reported in the Directory (FS029) file to their respective authorizers. There are two fields for charter authorizer identifiers in the Directory. These fields should be filled for each charter school submitted in the Directory file. In the Directory file, if the charter only has one authorizer, only fill out the first field and leave the second field blank. If the charter school has multiple authorizers, each authorizer should be reported in the Charter Authorizer Directory separately.
Can abbreviations be used in the name?

Do other files collect related data?
Yes. Files 037 and 134 collect information on LEAs that receive Title I, Part A funds.

File 037 collects information on the number of students participating in and served by programs operated by LEAs under Title I, Part A. File 134 collects information on the number of students participating in and served by school-level Title I, Part A, programs.
When does a State report the permitted value of “Missing”?

If an amount for an LEA is unavailable, a State includes a record for the LEA in the file and reports “-1” for the missing dollar value. A State is expected to have dollar values for each LEA reported for each data group.

If a State reports a value of Missing for one or more LEAs, the State should include a data note that describes the circumstances that resulted in the data not being available in the explanation field.
If an EDFacts Coordinator has any questions about why a status is MISSING for a school or subgroup, the Coordinator should contact the State’s Title I, Part A Director.
What is the parent and family engagement reservation?

The parent and family engagement reservation under Title I, Part A, is the amount of Title I, Part A funds reserved by LEAs for parent and family engagement activities in schools and LEAs operating Title I, Part A programs. (ESEA section 1116(a)(3)).
What parent and family engagement reservation amounts are generally expected?

For an LEA with a Title I, Part A allocation greater than $500,000, a parental involvement reservation of at least one percent of the Title I, Part A allocation is required. For an LEA with a Title I, Part A allocation less than or equal to $500,000, a parent and family engagement reservation that exceeds zero percent of the Title I, Part A allocation is expected unless the LEA did not reserve any funds to carry out requirements in ESEA section 1116 (while still meeting applicable requirements for parent and family engagement).
Which LEAs should be included in this Data Group?
All LEAs that receive Title I, Part A funds are included in this Data Group.

What is an LEA’s Title I, Part A Allocation?

An LEA’s Title I, Part A allocation is the dollar amount of Title I, Part A funds awarded to an LEA by its SEA in accordance with the ESEA Title I requirements and implementing regulations. (ESEA sections 1124, 1124A, 1125, and 1125A; 34 C.F.R. §§ 200.70-75 and § 200.100).
How does an LEA’s federal fiscal year grant award correspond with the school year?

ED makes initial Title I, Part A awards to SEAs on July 1 and in turn SEAs award Title I, Part A funds to eligible LEAs for use primarily in the next school year. For example, ED awarded federal fiscal year 2025 Title I, Part A funds to SEAs on July 1, 2024, for use by SEAs and LEAs primarily in the 2025-26 school year. (Under Title I, Part A requirements, LEAs must obligate 85 percent of their fiscal year 2025 Title I, Part A funds by September 30, 2026, and any remaining funds by September 2027.) An SEA that is reporting on the 2025-26 school year reports an LEA’s federal fiscal year 2025 Title I, Part A grant award amount.
Which LEAs should be included in this Data Group?
All LEAs that receive Title I, Part A funds are included in this Data Group.

The responses in this section are based on guidance from the data stewards.
What students should be reported in Data Group 814?

For Data Group 814, include all students in grades Kindergarten through Grade 12, and comparable ungraded levels, who were enrolled in the school for at least 10 school days at any time during the school year, and who were absent 10% or more of the school days in the school in which they were enrolled.
What students should be reported in Data Group 887?

For Data Group 887, include all students in grades Kindergarten through Grade 12, and comparable ungraded levels, who were enrolled in an LEA within the state and a similar count for the SEA. Included students should be those who were enrolled for at least 10 school days at any time during the school year, and who were absent 10% or more of the school days in which they were enrolled. Counts should be unduplicated such that a student is only included once per LEA and once per SEA.

For Data Group 887, use the school-level determination of whether a student is chronically absent (i.e., a student who was enrolled at a school for 10 or more days and was absent 10% or more of those days or a student who was enrolled in a State institution for 60 or more days and was absent 10% or more of those days) to report the unduplicated count at the LEA- and SEA-level. If a student attended multiple schools, do not re-determine whether the student was chronically absent using the combined attendance across schools.
A student may be reported in multiple LEAs; please see “What is an unduplicated number of students?” below.
Please also see “Should state institutions be included in this file?” below.
Why are SEA and LEA counts reported for only two category sets, economically disadvantaged and homeless students?

The Office of Elementary and Secondary Education and the Office of Civil Rights co-steward this data file. Initially, only school level data were collected for the Civil Rights Data Collection, which is publicly reported at the school level. However, student outcomes including chronic absenteeism at the school, LEA and State-levels are relevant to OESE programs, such as Title I, Part A and the Education for Homeless Children and Youth program, which focus on serving economically disadvantaged students and homeless children and youth, respectively. For example, the Education for Homeless Children and Youth program uses student data at the State and LEA level to track program performance.
When are students considered absent?

Students are absent when they were not physically on school grounds and were not participating in instruction or instruction-related activities at an approved off-grounds location for at least half the school day. See definition of Chronic Student Absenteeism in section 2.6.
What is an unduplicated number of students?

Students are to be counted once at each school where they meets the definition of chronically absent. For example, if a student is enrolled in school A for half the school year and school B for the other half of the school year and is chronically absent in both schools, this student is counted as chronically absent at both school A and B.

Similarly, students are to be counted once at each LEA where they meet the definition of chronically absent. However, a student who attends multiple schools within an LEA is only counted once per LEA even if the student enrolls in multiple schools and is chronically absent while enrolled at multiple schools within the LEA. Likewise, a student is only counted once for the SEA count, even if the student was chronically absent while enrolled in multiple LEAs.
Is there a minimum number of days a student has to be enrolled before the student is counted as chronically absent?
Students should be counted in the Chronic Absenteeism data once they have been enrolled in a school for a minimum of 10 school days.
How is absence for a student who attends school part-time reported?

The absence for a part-time student is based on the student’s schedule instead of the school day. For example, if a student attends school normally for 4 hours daily, then an absence would be counted when a student is out of school two or more hours per the definition for absence included in section 2.6.
Which schools must be included in this file?

All public elementary and public secondary schools that were operational during the reporting school year should be included in this file. This includes schools with a school type of regular school, special education school, alternative school, or career and technical school. Not included in this file are operational schools that did not have one or more students for the reporting period, or closed, inactive, or future schools (which are not considered operational schools for the reporting school year). Entities with a school type of "reportable program” are also not considered operational schools.
Are State institutions counted in this file?

Yes, States should include State institutions (e.g. juvenile justice schools and department of health services schools) in their Chronic Absenteeism data. Student must be enrolled in a State institution for 60 school days before Chronic Absenteeism starts being collected.
What if the unduplicated number of students absent 10% or more school days during the school year is not available?

Are all charter schools included in this file?

No. The state must report a charter contract that has an ID number, an approval date and a renewal date for all operational charter schools. The state may optionally report a charter contract for inactive or future schools.
When a state does not assign identification codes to charter schools, can the School ID or NCES ID be used for reporting? Why?

No. States should assign a unique identifier that corresponds to each separate and distinct charter contract and enter this unique number in the Charter contract ID number field. These data will enable the Department and other stakeholders to understand the full universe of charters which are executed by authorized public chartering agencies in each state.

The purpose of the charter contract ID number (DG830) is to assign a unique identifier to each charter or contract between an authorized public chartering agency (see definition in Section 2.6) and the organization that holds the charter. In some cases, each charter contract corresponds to one and only one charter school. However, in many cases, a single charter contract captures two or more charter schools.
If there is no change in the charter contract approval or renewal date, is it necessary to report these data each year?
Yes. While some dates will not change, it is possible that some event may occur that could result in changes to these dates.
Is the contract approval date the first date the contract was signed, or the most recent date the contract was renewed?

The purpose of the “Charter Contract Approval Date” is to capture and maintain the date of execution of a charter school’s current contract with its authorizer. For a relatively new school, which has not reached its renewal date, this date will correspond with the effective date of the school’s current contract with its authorizer. For a charter school that has a contract that has been renewed, the “Charter Contract Approval Date” will correspond with that renewal date, as that date would represent the effective date of the charter school’s current charter or contract with the authorizer. In that case, the “Charter Contract Renewal Date” would represent the new renewal date for the current contract.

Do other files collect related data?
Yes.

The Accountability Metadata Collection (FS5019, FS5020, FS5021, FS5022, FS5023, and FS5024) collects information to support the collection and interpretation of data reported for ESEA Title I accountability indicators (FS199, FS200, FS201, FS202 and FS205). Specifically, in the Accountability Metadata Collection, a State will report for all indicator measures the State uses for ESEA Title I accountability, as defined in the State’s approved ESEA consolidated State plan for the reporting year. For each indicator, the State will report:

A State also provides the name of any State-defined subgroups that were reported as options in the category Major Racial and Ethnic Groups (Accountability). See the EDPass Accountability Metadata User Guidehttps://www.ed.gov/data/edfacts-initiative/edfacts-resources/edpass-metadata-documentation for more specific information.

FS200, FS202, and FS205 collect information for all public schools on Academic Achievement, School Quality or Student Success, and Progress in Achieving English Language Proficiency indicators a State uses for ESEA Title I accountability, as defined in the State's approved ESEA consolidated State plan for the reporting year. FS201 collects information for public schools that do not offer a 12th grade on the Other Academic indicator measure(s) for Elementary and Secondary Schools that are Not High Schools a State uses for ESEA Title I accountability.

FS206 and FS212 collect information about the identification of schools for support and improvement on school and subgroup performance for each of the indicators the State uses for ESEA Title I accountability.

FS151 collects the numbers of students in the adjusted cohorts for a State’s four-year adjusted cohort graduation rate and the numbers of students in the adjusted cohorts for any extended-year ACGRs adopted by the State. FS150 collects a State’s four-year adjusted cohort graduation rates and the State’s extended-year adjusted cohort graduation rates any extended-year ACGRs adopted by the State.
Which schools are included in this file?
ESEA section 8101(28) defines a high school is as a secondary school that grants a diploma, as defined by the State, and includes, at least, grade 12.

A State reports for all public schools that offer a 12th grade that were operational during the reporting year. This includes regular schools, charter schools, magnet schools, special education schools, career and technical education schools, alternative education schools, and any other type of public school in the State.

A submission to EDFacts of a file that does not include all public schools with a 12th grade that were operational during the reporting year and had at least one student in a cohort for an Adjusted Cohort Graduation Rate (ACGR) is considered not complete.
How are data a State reports for ESEA Title I accountability related to the State’s approved ESEA consolidated State plan for the reporting year?

The data a State reports for ESEA Title I accountability must be consistent with the State’s ESEA Title I accountability system described in the State’s approved ESEA consolidated State plan for the reporting year.
What definitions must a State use for graduation cohorts for ACGR purposes?
A State must calculate and report a graduation cohort based on a four-year adjusted cohort as specified in ESEA section 8101(25). The four-year adjusted cohort is defined as follows:

The number of first-time students in grade 9 enrolled in a high school no later than the date by which student membership data is collected annually by the SEA for submission to the Department’s National Center for Educational Statistics (i.e., on or about October 1), adjusted by adding into the cohort any student who transfers in later during grade 9 or during the next three years, plus any student expected to receive a State-defined alternate diplomaThe State-defined alternate diploma is explained in more detail in subsequent questions. who was reassigned to the cohort, and subtracting any student from the cohort who transfers out, emigrates to another country, transfers to a prison or juvenile facility, or dies during that same period.

A State may, at its discretion, adopt one or more extended-year ACGR as specified in section 8101(23) of the ESEA as part of its ESEA Title I accountability system in its approved ESEA consolidated State plan for the reporting year. If a State has adopted such an extended-year ACGR, it must report cohort data for each extended-year ACGR separately from the four-year ACGR. The extended-year adjusted cohort is defined as follows:

The number of first-time students in grade 9 enrolled in a high school no later than the date by which student membership data is collected annually by the SEA for submission to the Department’s National Center for Educational Statistics (i.e., on or about October 1), adjusted by adding into the cohort any student who transfers in later during grade 9 or during the subsequent years in the time period of the extended rate, plus any student expected to receive a State-defined alternate diploma who was reassigned to the cohort, and subtracting any student from the cohort who transfers out, emigrates to another country, transfers to a prison or juvenile facility, or dies during that same period.
For how many Graduation Rate indicator measures are data reported?

For all applicable schools and subgroups within the State (see Table 2.2-1 and the Q&A “Which schools are included in this file?”), a State reports data for each school and each subgroup in each school for each Graduation Rate indicator measure defined by the State. Each State has defined at least one Graduation Rate indicator measure in the State’s approved ESEA consolidated State plan for the reporting year. Some States also have defined more than one Graduation Rate indicator measure. A State may report data for up to 3 Graduation Rate indicators measures.
How are the indicator measures reported?

A State reports its first indicator measure using the permitted value “GRM01” and any additional indicator measures using the available, sequential, permitted values (e.g., “GRM02”, “GRM03”). For example, if a State determines that “GRM01” is its indicator measure for its four-year ACGR and “GRM02” is its indicator measure for its five-year ACGR, “GRM01” is always used for data for the Graduation Rate indicator measure for the four-year ACGR, and “GRM02” is always used for data for the five-year ACGR indicator measure.

For example, if the State reports school performance for the Graduation Rate indicator measure for the four-year ACGR as GRM01, then the State will describe the indicator measure GRM01 in the Accountability Metadata Collection as the measure for the four-year ACGR.
How is State-defined status for an indicator measure reported?

For each school or subgroup for which a State reports a status for the Graduation Rate indicator of “State defined status”, the State must also report the performance of the school or subgroup in the field “State Defined Status Indicator.”
The Accountability Metadata Survey includes questions about the type of scale for the indicator measure:

The data in the field “State Defined Status Indicator” must align to the responses in the Accountability Metadata Survey. For example, if the file has percentages in the field “State Defined Status Indicator” for GRM01, the scale type in the Accountability Metadata Survey would be “Interval – Percentage scale.”
When does a State report the permitted value of “too few students” for a school or subgroup?

In cases where, for a school as a whole or a subgroup within a school, the number of students is less than the State’s minimum group size for ESEA Title I accountability, as defined in the State’s approved ESEA consolidated State plan for the reporting year, a State reports the permitted value of “too few students” for the school and/or subgroup. For example, if a State has defined a minimum group size for ESEA Title I accountability of 30 students, the State will report a permitted value of “too few students” for a school or subgroup for which results are available for less than 30 students for the reporting year.
When does a State report the permitted value of “no students in the subgroup” for a school or subgroup”?
In cases where there are no students in a school or subgroup, a State reports the permitted value of “no students in the subgroup” for the school and/or a subgroup.

If there are no students in subgroup for the indicator measure in a school, the State reports a permitted value of “no students in the subgroup”. For example, a State reports a permitted value of “no students in the subgroup” for the English learner subgroup for a school in which zero English learners were enrolled for the reporting year.
When does a State report the permitted value of “MISSING”?

If the status of a school's performance for an indicator measure is unavailable, a State includes a record for the school in the file and reports a permitted value of MISSING for the school or subgroup. A State is expected to have information on the indicator status of all schools and all subgroups in a school and to report a permitted value of State-defined status, too few students, or no students in the subgroup for each school and each subgroup in each school in the State.

If a State reports a permitted value of MISSING for one or more schools or subgroups in a school, the State should include a data note that describes the circumstances that resulted in the data not being available in the State Submission Plan.
Which permitted values should be used for the category Major Racial and Ethnic Groups (Accountability)?
A State uses the major racial and ethnic groups defined for ESEA Title I accountability in the State’s approved ESEA consolidated State plan for the reporting year.

Inexperienced Status

This section contains guidance for submitting this file in the format of questions and answers. The first section is guidance that applies to the entire file. Then each aggregation has a separate section.
The questions in this section are based on the following statute and/or regulatory guidance: Section 1111(h)(5)(D) of the ESEAhttps://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/COMPS-748/pdf/COMPS-748.pdf.
How are staff reported?

Report staff in terms of FTE (full-time equivalent). FTE should be counted in hundredths. For example, if a teaching position is filled by four people, each working the same amount of time, each person would count as 0.25 FTE. The total FTE counts for instructional staff must be reported to the nearest hundredth, with an EXPLICIT decimal (e.g., 59.20).
How are teachers reported who work at multiple schools during the school year?

There is no specific methodology that a state is required to use for reporting a teacher who worked at multiple schools during the school year. However, the reporting requirement is based on FTE to provide states with the maximum flexibility to report these data as accurately as possible. For example, a state may choose to either associate the full FTE at the school where the teacher spent the majority of their time, or they may choose to divide the FTE across the schools where they spent their time based on the proportion of time spent at each school.
Which teachers should be included in this file?

This file should include all public school teachers, whether they taught full-time or part-time. It should include teachers teaching all subjects and all grades. It should not include paraprofessionals.
Is the percentage of teachers reported?

No. While section 1111(h)(5)(D) of the ESEA requires States to report on the “number and percentage” of teachers, States will not be reporting a percentage to ED. By reporting the FTE values for each category set as well as an education unit total, ED will be able to calculate percentages using the education unit total as the denominator.
Do each of the aggregations equal the Education Unit Total?
Yes. The FTE total of teachers by inexperienced status, by emergency or provisional credential status, and by out of field status should equal the FTE reported as the Education Unit Total.
What is the definition of inexperienced?

Section 1111(h)(5)(D)(i) of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act requires States to report on “inexperienced teachers” but does not define “inexperienced.” Therefore, States have the authority to define what it means to be inexperienced.
What is the definition of an emergency or provisional credential?
There is no specific definition in the Elementary and Secondary Education Act. Therefore, States have the authority to define an emergency or provisional credential.
Are emergency credentials reported separately from provisional credentials?

No. This reporting requirement is aligned with the reporting requirement in section 1111(h)(5)(D) of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, as amended, which requires States to report to the Secretary “the number and percentage of teachers teaching with emergency or provisional credentials.” States must report on teachers teaching with emergency or provisional credentials as one combined value.
What is the definition of out of field?

There is no specific definition in the Elementary and Secondary Education Act. Therefore, States have the authority to define what it means to be “not teaching in the subject or field for which the teacher is certified or licensed.”
How should a teacher be reported if they are considered to be teaching out of field for only some classes?

There is no specific methodology that a state is required to use for reporting a teacher who is considered to be teaching out of field for certain classes but is considered to be teaching in their field for other classes. However, the reporting requirement is based on FTE to provide states with the maximum flexibility to report these data as accurately as possible. For example, a state might consider it to be most accurate to divide their FTE across permitted values to reflect that they are teaching partially in-field.

Do other files collect related data?
Yes.

The Accountability Metadata Collection (FS5019, FS5020, FS5021, FS5022, FS5023, and FS5024) collects information to support the collection and interpretation of data reported for ESEA Title I accountability indicators (FS199, FS200, FS201, FS202 and FS205). Specifically, in the Accountability Metadata Collection, a State will report for all indicator measures the State uses for ESEA Title I accountability, as defined in the State’s approved ESEA consolidated State plan for the reporting year, and, for each indicator, the State reports:
See the EDPass Accountability Metadata User Guidehttps://www.ed.gov/data/edfacts-initiative/edfacts-resources/edpass-metadata-documentation for more specific information.

FS199, FS200, FS201 and FS202 collect information on the other indicators a State uses for ESEA Title I accountability, as defined in the State's approved ESEA consolidated State plan for the reporting year.

FS206 and FS212 collect information about the identification of schools for support and improvement on school and subgroup performance for each of the indicators the State uses for ESEA Title I accountability.
Which schools are included in this file?

A State reports for all public schools that were operational during the reporting year. This includes regular schools, charter schools, magnet schools, special education schools, career and technical education schools, alternative education schools, and any other type of public school in the State.
A submission to EDFacts of a file that does not include all operational public schools is considered not complete.
How are data a State reports for ESEA Title I accountability related to the State’s approved ESEA consolidated State plan for the reporting year?

The data a State reports for ESEA Title I accountability must be consistent with the State’s ESEA Title I accountability system described in the State’s approved ESEA consolidated State plan for the reporting year.
For how many Progress in Achieving English Language Proficiency indicator measures are data reported?

For all applicable schools and subgroups within the State (see Table 2.2-1 and the Q&A “Which schools are included in this file?”), a State reports data for each school and each subgroup in each school for each Progress in Achieving English Language Proficiency indicator measure defined by the State. Each State has defined at least one Progress in Achieving English Language Proficiency indicator measure in the State’s approved ESEA consolidated State plan for the reporting year. Some States also have defined more than one Progress in Achieving English Language Proficiency indicator measure A State may report data for up to 2 Progress in Achieving English Language Proficiency indicators measures.
How are the indicator measures reported?

A State reports its first Progress in Achieving English Language Proficiency indicator measure using the permitted value “PAELP1” and, if applicable, its second Progress in Achieving English Language Proficiency indicator measure using the permitted value “PAELP2”.
The State will provide the name(s) and description(s) for each indicator measure in the Accountability Metadata Survey.
How is State-defined status for an indicator measure reported?

For each school for which a State reports a status for progress in Achieving English Language Proficiency indicator measure of “State defined status”, the State must also report the performance of the school in the field “State Defined Status Indicator.”
The Accountability Metadata Survey includes questions about the type of scale for the indicator:

The data in the field “State Defined Status Indicator” must align to the responses in the Accountability Metadata Survey. For example, if the file has percentages in the field “State Defined Status Indicator” for PAELP1, the scale type in the Accountability Metadata Survey would be “Interval – Percentage scale.”
When does a State report the permitted value of “too few students” for a school?

In cases where the number of students is less than the State’s minimum group size for ESEA Title I accountability, as defined in the State’s approved ESEA consolidated State plan for the reporting year, a State reports the permitted value of “too few students” for the school using the Progress Achieving English Language Proficiency Measure 1 (PAELP1). For example, if a State has defined a minimum group size for ESEA Title I accountability of 30 students, the State will report a permitted value of “too few students” for a school for which results are available for less than 30 students for the reporting year.
When does a State report the permitted value of “no students in the subgroup” for a school?

In cases where there are no English learners in a school, a State reports the permitted value of “no students in the subgroup” for the school for the reporting year using the Progress Achieving English Language Proficiency Measure 1 (PAELP1).
When does a State report the permitted value of “MISSING”?

If the status of a school's performance for an indicator measure is unavailable, a State includes a record for the school in the file and reports a permitted value of MISSING for the school using the Progress Achieving English Language Proficiency Measure 1 (PAELP1). Other indicators can be left out of the file. A State is expected to have information on the indicator status of all schools and to report a permitted value of State-defined status, too few students, or no students in the subgroup for each school in the State.

If a State reports a permitted value of MISSING for one or more schools the State should include a data note that describes the circumstances that resulted in the data not being available in the State Submission Plan.
If an EDFacts Coordinator has any questions about why a status is MISSING for a school, the Coordinator should contact the State’s Title I, Part A Director.

This section contains guidance for submitting this file in the format of questions and answers.
EDFacts Coordinator should contact the State’s Title I, Part A Director before beginning work on this FS.
Do other files collect related data?
Yes. FS212 collects the reasons for school support and improvement statuses.
Which schools must be included in this file?

All public schools that were operational during the school year for which data are reported. This includes regular schools, charter schools, magnet schools, special education schools, career and technical education schools, alternative education schools, and any other type of public school in the State. Submissions that do not include all public schools are considered not complete.
For what reporting year does a State report school statuses for this file?

A State reports school identification statuses for the school year of data on which the identification statuses are based. For example, for SY 2023-2024 for this file, an SEA reports the Comprehensive Support and Improvement (CSI), Targeted Support and Improvement (TSI), and/or Additional Targeted Support and Improvement (ATSI) identification statuses that apply to schools for the SY 2024-2025 based on school performance data from SY 2023-2024 (i.e., the reporting year).
How should schools identified for support and improvement for multiple years be included in this file?

Schools identified for Comprehensive Support and Improvement (CSI), Targeted Support and Improvement (TSI), and Additional Targeted Support and Improvement (ATSI) should be included in the file by those statuses for every year that they are in those statuses. For example, if a CSI school is identified for three years, it should be reported as a CSI school in this file for each of the three years that it is in that status. A school’s initial identification may be based on data from an earlier school year.
How should states report schools that have been identified into a state-specific category of schools?

For purposes of reporting in this file, only schools that meet the statutory definitions of Comprehensive Support and Improvement (CSI), Targeted Support and Improvement (TSI), and/or Additional Targeted Support and Improvement (ATSI) should be reported as such. Schools in exit status should be reported in the appropriate exit status. All other schools should be reported as not CSI, not TSI, or not ATSI. If a state has state-specific rules for labeling schools as CSI, TSI, or ATSI that are in addition to those that are identified based on the statutory definitions, the schools that are only identified based on the state-specific rules should not be labeled as CSI, TSI, or ATSI schools. Instead, those schools should be reported as not CSI, not TSI, or not ATSI.
How should the exit status be used?

CSI and ATSI schools are reported with the exit status permitted value for the SY in which the schools met State-defined exit criteria. For example, if a CSI school met State-defined exit criteria based on school performance data for 2023-2024, the State reports the school as “Comprehensive Support and Improvement – Exit Status” for SY 2023-2024. Because the ESEA does not require exit criteria for TSI schools, an exit status does not apply to TSI schools.
How should the missing status be used?
A State is expected to determine an accountability status for all public schools. If a status is missing for any school, the State should:

The missing status should only be used in the rare instance that the State was unable to determine the support and improvement status for the school due to extenuating circumstances. Missing status should not be used for schools that were included in the State’s ESEA Title I accountability system but were not identified for support and improvement or for schools included in the State’s system of Annual Meaningful Differentiation using a different methodology for schools for which an accountability determination cannot otherwise be made, as described in the State’s approved ESEA consolidated State plan.

How does a State report support and improvement statuses when a school is identified for multiple statuses (e.g., Comprehensive Support and Improvement (CSI), Targeted Support and Improvement (TSI) and/Additional Targeted Support and Improvement (ATSI)?

A State reports all statuses that apply to a school. A State is not required to include a school in more than one status. If a State chooses to apply more than one status to a school (e.g., CSI and ATSI), the State reports all statuses for the school. For example, a school could be identified for CSI based on overall performance and could simultaneously be identified for ATSI based on the performance of subgroup A. In this case, the State reports both identification statuses for the school. This also applies to schools in an exit status. For example, if a school is in ATSI exit status and identified for CSI, a State reports the school in both statuses (i.e., ADDLTSIEXIT and CSI)

English Learners Proficiency Within Five Years Status
The proficiency status of English Learners within five years.
This section contains guidance for submitting this file in the format of questions and answers.

The questions in this section are based on the following regulations and/or regulatory guidance: Section 3121(a)(6) of the ESEA, questions J1-3 of Title III guidance and 34 C.F.R. 200.6(h)(1)(ii))https://www2.ed.gov/policy/elsec/leg/essa/essatitleiiiguidenglishlearners10219.pdf.
Which students should not be reported in this file?

If, in the reporting school year (SY), a student is listed as an English learner (EL) whose parent opted their child out of participation in a language instruction educational program (LIEP) in an LEA receiving Title III funds, then that child would not be included in this data group.
ELs who have not yet attained proficiency on the annual ELP assessment but have been in EL status for less than five years are not included in this data group.
What students are included as “Proficient within five years?”

For the number of students reported as “Proficient within five years (PROF5YRSYES),” an LEA that receives Title III funds must report on all students who attained proficiency on the annual ELP assessment in the current reporting SY and who were within five years of identification as an EL and first enrollment in the LEA.

For example, reporting the SY 2025-26 count of proficient within five years (PROF5YRSYES) ELs, an LEA would identify students who attained proficiency on the annual ELP assessment and who were first identified as ELs in an LEA receiving Title III funds in SY 2021-22, SY 2022-23, SY 2023-24, SY 2024-25 or SY 2025-26.

The Proficient within five years (PROF5YRSYES) count for the 2025-26 reporting SY must not include any students who were first identified as an EL and first enrolled in the LEA prior to SY 2021-22, as that would be beyond the parameters for reporting for the 2025-26 reporting SY. The Proficient within five years (PROF5YRSYES) count also must not include students whose were listed in the 2025-26 reporting SY as an EL whose parent opted their child out of LIEP participation, as noted above.
What students are included as “Not proficient within five years?”

For the number of students reported as “Not proficient within five years (PROF5YRSNO),” an LEA that receives Title III funds must report on all ELs who have not attained proficiency on the annual ELP assessment within five years of identification as an EL and first enrollment in the LEA. An EL must be reported in the Not proficient within five years (PROF5YRSNO) count if, by the end of the 12-month reporting period, the student is in his or her 5th year or beyond of identification as an EL and has not attained English language proficiency on the annual ELP assessment by the end of the 5th year.

For example, for reporting the SY 2025-26 count of Not proficient within five years (PROF5YRSNO), an LEA that receives Title III funds would determine which EL students enrolled during the 2025-26 reporting SY were first identified as ELs in SY 2021-22 or earlier, and then report how many of those students had not attained proficiency on the annual ELP assessment by the end of the 12-month reporting period.

For an EL to be included in the Not proficient within five years (PROF5YRSNO) count for the 2025-26 reporting SY it does not matter what year prior to SY 2021-22 the student was first identified as an EL and first enrolled in the LEA, as long as the EL had not attained proficiency on the annual ELP assessment by the end of the 12-month reporting period.
ELs who were not assessed on the annual ELP assessment in their fifth year (the reporting SY) must be included in the Not proficient within five years (PROF5YRSNO) count.

The Not proficient within five years (PROF5YRSNO) count must not include students whose were listed in the 2025-26 reporting SY as an EL whose parent opted their child out of LIEP participation, as noted above.
Do students have to be enrolled in a Title III LEA for all 5 years in order to be included in this data group?

No. As stated above, LEAs that receive Title III funds must report on all ELs who have attained and not attained proficiency on the annual ELP assessment within five years of (1) identification as an English learner and (2) first enrollment in the LEA. This reporting requirement does not require that a student is enrolled in the same LEA for all 5 years in order to be included. LEAs receiving Title III funds should include ELs who (1) first enroll in their LEA and then (2) transfer to another LEA and then (3) transfer back to their LEA. See scenario 1 below for an example. In this example, , which uses SY 2025-26 as the reporting year, the LEA would not reset the identification timeline when the EL re-enrolls in their LEA.
Table 2.5-1: Scenario 1

ED acknowledges that LEAs may be unable to accurately track an EL’s identification timeline for students who transfer in and out of their LEA. In these cases, the LEA receiving Title III funds may choose to reset the identification timeline for ELs re-entering their LEA. See scenario 2 below for an example.
Table 2.5-2: Scenario 2
LEAs receiving Title III funds must reset the identification timeline for ELs entering their LEA for the first time, even though they were previously identified as an EL in another LEA.

LEAs should use Kindergarten as the first year of identification and not preschool, for purposes of reporting for this file specification.
Is English language proficiency measured the same way in FS210 and FS211?

No. For FS210, English language proficiency is measured by the annual ELP assessment, while for FS211, English language proficiency is measured by exit from EL status, which may include additional state criteria.

What students are included in the English Learners Exited Status (EXTDYES ) count?

For the number of students report as English Learners Exited Status (EXTDYES) count, LEAs that receive Title III funds must report on English learners who were served by an LIEP and who, by the end of the 12-month reporting period, had exited EL status based on attainment of English language proficiency. For reporting the SY 2025-26 count of students that Did not exit (EXTDNO) ELs, identify students who were in EL status and in LIEPs in LEAs receiving Title III funds during SY 2025-26 and who did not exit EL status by the end of the SY 2025-26 reporting period.

How should data be reported when a school has more than one reason for identification?
Report all reasons for identification. Include each reason in a separate row in the file.

How does a State report reasons for identification for a school if the school is identified for more than one support and improvement category (i.e., Comprehensive Support and Improvement (CSI), Targeted Support and Improvement (TSI) and/or Additional Targeted Support and Improvement (ATSI)?

A State reports the reasons for identification for all support and improvement statuses for which a school is identified. This includes, as applicable, reasons for identification in DG 866 (Comprehensive support identification table), DG 867 (Targeted support identification table) and DG 888 (Additional Targeted support identification table). For example, a school could be identified for CSI based on overall performance and could simultaneously be identified for TSI based on the performance of subgroup A. In this case, a State reports the reasons for both designations for the school.
How should a school reported as in exit status in FS206 be reported in this file if the school also is identified in another status?

A State reports a school reported as in exit status in FS206 in this file only if the school also is identified in another status. For example, a school that is in Comprehensive Support and Improvement (CSI) exit status but newly identified for Targeted Support and Improvement (TSI) would be included in this file for its TSI status only. A school that is reported in an exit status in FS206 and has not been identified for any other status is not included in this file.
What if data on identification reasons is missing?

A State is expected to submit a reason for identification for all public schools reported in FS206 with an accountability status of Comprehensive Support and Improvement (CSI), Targeted Support and Improvement (TSI) or Additional Targeted Support and Improvement (ATSI, reported as ADDLTSI). If a State is missing the reason for identification for any school, the State should include a data note in the State Submission Plan (SSP) indicating that some schools are missing a reason for identification.

A business rule will fail when an identification reason is not provided for a school a State reports with an accountability status of CSI, TSI, or ATSI in FS206. In a data note for any such rule failure, a State should explain the extenuating circumstances that resulted in not having an identification reason for the school.

A State should use the major racial and ethnic subgroups defined for Title I accountability in the State’s ESEA consolidated State plan for the reporting year.

Which students should be reported in this file?
Report only students who during the reporting period:
Are programs funded by Title I, Part A reported in this file?
No. Do not report programs funded solely through Title I, Part A.
What programs may receive Title I, Part D Subpart 1 funds?
Under ESEA section 1411, a State agency is eligible for assistance under subpart 1 if such State agency is responsible for providing free public education for children and youth—
Revised! Can a student attain multiple outcomes during the reporting year?

Yes. For example, a student might earn course credits and obtain a diploma or enroll in a GED program. The student would be counted once in each outcome attained. Students who earn high school course credits and earn a diploma, or who enroll in a GED program and earn a GED, should be counted once in each of those categories.
Can a student earn an academic / career and technical outcome more than once during the reporting year?

Yes. Students can earn an academic or career and technical outcome more than once during the reporting year but should only be counted once in this outcome (e.g., a student who earned 5 course credits after exiting would be reported as 1 student earning high school course credits in this file).
If a student also obtained high school course credits while in the facility or program, they should be counted in file specification FS218 (N or D in Program Outcomes – State Agency).
Exceptions would be for the following outcomes which can only be obtained once:
New! What types of courses or programs should be reported under the category ENROLLTRAIN (Enrolled in job training courses/programs)?

State Agencies should report any type of career or technical education course or program that provides students with the opportunity to gain knowledge or skills that may be applied to industry-recognized credentials or certification,
New! Should the outcome data be broken out by neglected and delinquent, or by different program categories?
No. For this file, all students served by Title I, Part D Subpart 1 programs and attaining outcomes while in the program and during the reported year should be reported together.

Yes. There are several file specifications that are used to collect data on Title I, Part D. The EDFacts Workbookhttps://www.ed.gov/data/edfacts-initiative/edfacts-resources/edfacts-workbook contains a list of the data groups that support oversight and reporting of the Prevention and Intervention Programs for the Education of Children and Youth Who Are Neglected, Delinquent or At-Risk Program (N or D). This file is used to collect data on academic / career and technical outcome attainment at exit or up to 90 days after exit from the program (but not during enrollment in the program). FS218 (N or D in Program Outcomes – State Agency) is used to collect data on outcome attainment achieved while students are enrolled in the program funded by Title I, Part D Subpart 1.
Revised! Should State- and LEA-level data match?
No. The State and LEA levels of this file count two different populations of students.
See the EDFacts Workbookhttps://www.ed.gov/data/edfacts-initiative/edfacts-resources/edfacts-workbook for the standard definitions. The following definitions support this file:
Adult correctional institution —a facility in which persons (including persons under 21 years of age) are confined as a result of a conviction for a criminal offense.
Community day program— a regular program of instruction provided by a State agency at a community day school operated specifically for neglected or delinquent children and youth.
Institution for delinquent children and youth means, as determined by the SEA, a public or private residential facility that is operated primarily for the care of children and youth who –
(i) Have been adjudicated to be delinquent or in need of supervision; and
(ii) Have had an average length of stay in the institution of at least 30 days.

Institution for neglected children and youth means, as determined by the SEA, a public or private residential facility, other than a foster home, that is operated primarily for the care of children and youth who –
(i) Have been committed to the institution or voluntarily placed in the institution under applicable State law due to abandonment, neglect, or death of their parents or guardians; and
(ii) Have had an average length of stay in the institution of at least 30 days.

Regular program of instruction means an educational program (not beyond grade 12) in an institution or a community day program for neglected or delinquent children that consists of classroom instruction in basic school subjects such as reading, mathematics, and career and technical education, and that is supported by non-Federal funds. Neither the manufacture of goods within the institution nor activities related to institutional maintenance are considered classroom instruction.

Enrollment counts of students in foster care are reported for all LEAs that receive Title I, Part A funds.
For which students in foster care are enrollment counts reported?

The counts reported are the numbers of students in foster care enrolled in LEAs that receive Title I, Part A funds. The Title I, Part A foster care requirements apply to all students in foster care enrolled in an LEA that receives Title I, Part A funds, even when these students may not be served by or eligible for Title I, Part A services in a school-level Title I, Part A schoolwide program or targeted assistance program.
Should an LEA count a student in foster care if the student was not in foster care for an entire school year?
Yes. Each LEA enrollment count should include students who were in foster care at any point, and for any length of time, while enrolled in the LEA during the reporting year.

Students in Foster Care

DG22 - Title I school status:
Title I School Status

An indication that a school is designated under state and federal regulations as being eligible for participation in programs authorized by Title I of ESEA as amended and whether it has a Title I program.
This section contains guidance for submitting this file in the format of questions and answers.
Do other files collect related data?

Yes. FS037 (Title I Part A SWP/TAS Participation) and FS134 (Title I Part A Participation) collect LEA- and SEA-level data on the numbers of students participating in Title I, Part A schoolwide programs and targeted assistance programs.

LEAs with schools reported with a status of Title I targeted assistance school or Title I schoolwide school for FS223/DG22 are expected to report counts of students served in Title I targeted assistance program schools or Title I schoolwide program school for FS037 and FS134.
Which schools must be included in this file?

All public elementary or public secondary school that were operational during the reporting school year should be included in this file. This includes schools with a school type of regular school, special education school, alternative school, or career and technical school. Closed, inactive, or future schools are not considered operational schools for the reporting school year. Entities with a school type of "reportable program” also are not considered operational schools.
When is a school’s status Title I targeted assistance school or Title I schoolwide school?
A school that receives Title I, Part A funds operates a Title I targeted assistance program or a Title I schoolwide.

A school’s status is Title I targeted assistance school or Title I schoolwide school when the school is eligible for and receives Title I, Part A funds and operates a Title I targeted assistance program or a Title I schoolwide program during the regular school year (i.e., the instructional period not including intersession or summer sessions).
When is a school’s status Title I schoolwide eligible school-No program or Title I targeted assistance eligible school-No program?

A school’s status is Title I schoolwide eligible school-No program or Title I targeted assistance eligible school-No program when the school is eligible to receive Title I, Part A funds, but does not receive an allocation of Title I, Part A funds for the regular school year (i.e., the instructional period not including intersession or summer sessions).
Where is more information available about determining a school’s eligibility for Title I funds and within-LEA allocation of funds to schools?

More information on determining a school’s eligibility for Title I, Part A funds and within-LEA allocations is provided in the Department’s Within-District Allocations Under Title I, Part A of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965, as Amended, Non-Regulatory Guidance (February 2022), which is available at OESE’s Within District Allocations Under Title I report.https://oese.ed.gov/files/2022/02/Within-district-allocations-FINAL.pdf

DG868 - N or D assessment proficiency table - state agency:
Academic Subject (Assessment - no science)
The description of the content or subject area of an assessment.
Proficiency Status
An indication of whether scores were proficient or above.
This section contains guidance for submitting this file in the format of questions and answers.
The questions in this section are based on the following statute and/or regulatory guidance: ESEA sections 1411, 1431 and 1432 (3).
Which students should be reported in this file?

Report only students who received Title I, Part D, Subpart 1 services during the reporting period. This may include students who exited the N or D program during the reporting period, or who completed the assessment while in the program.
What if I do not have access to statewide assessment results for students who have exited Title I, Part D programs?

Reporting on this file is optional in the event that data is not available for students who have exited N or D programs. This data is intended to supplement the data collected on academic achievement in FS113 and FS125.
Are programs funded by Title I, Part A reported in this file?
No. Do not report programs funded solely through Title I, Part A.
What programs may receive Title I, Part D Subpart 1 funds?
Under ESEA section 1411, a State agency is eligible for assistance under subpart 1 if such State agency is responsible for providing free public education for children and youth—
What assessments should be reported?

Report any assessment reported in FS175 (Academic Achievement in Mathematics) and any assessment reported in FS178 (Academic Achievement in Reading / Language Arts), including alternate assessments based on alternate academic achievement standards. Do not include the results of the Annual English language proficiency assessment taken in lieu of the statewide reading / language arts assessment.
What if my state assigns non-participants to the lowest level of proficiency?
Those students are not reported in these files (for reporting academic achievement results).
Are students who were not enrolled for the full academic year included in this file?
Yes. Include both students who were enrolled for the full academic year and those who were not enrolled for the full academic year in this file.
See the EDFacts Workbookhttps://www.ed.gov/data/edfacts-initiative/edfacts-resources/edfacts-workbook for the standard definitions. The following definitions support this file:
Adult correctional institution —a facility in which persons (including persons under 21 years of age) are confined as a result of a conviction for a criminal offense.
Community day program— a regular program of instruction provided by a State agency at a community day school operated specifically for neglected or delinquent children and youth.
Institution for delinquent children and youth means, as determined by the SEA, a public or private residential facility that is operated primarily for the care of children and youth who -
(i) Have been adjudicated to be delinquent or in need of supervision; and(ii) Have had an average length of stay in the institution of at least 30 days.

Institution for neglected children and youth means, as determined by the SEA, a public or private residential facility, other than a foster home, that is operated primarily for the care of children and youth who -

(i) Have been committed to the institution or voluntarily placed in the institution under applicable State law due to abandonment, neglect, or death of their parents or guardians; and(ii) Have had an average length of stay in the institution of at least 30 days.

Regular program of instruction means an educational program (not beyond grade 12) in an institution or a community day program for neglected or delinquent children that consists of classroom instruction in basic school subjects such as reading, mathematics, and career and technical education, and that is supported by non-Federal funds. Neither the manufacture of goods within the institution nor activities related to institutional maintenance are considered classroom instruction.

The unduplicated number of students who met the state criteria for classification as economically disadvantaged according to the state definition.

Do other files collect related data?

Yes. FS033 (Free and Reduced Price Lunch) collects information on the unduplicated number of students who are eligible to participate in the Free Lunch and Reduced-Price Lunch Programs under the National School Lunch Act of 1946 (DG565) and the unduplicated number of students in membership whose National School Lunch Program (NSLP) eligibility has been determined through direct certification (DG813).
Which schools must be included in this file?

All public elementary and public secondary schools that were operational during the reporting school year should be included in this file. This includes schools with a school type of regular school, special education school, alternative school, or career and technical school. Not included in this file are operational schools that did not have one or more students for the reporting period, or closed, inactive, or future schools (which are not considered operational schools for the reporting school year). Entities with a school type of "reportable program” are also not considered operational schools.
Which students are included in this file?
All students that the SEA regards as enrolled as elementary or secondary students are included in this file. In most cases, this includes students who are ungraded.
